claims.text: The unmodified (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy has a large caloric response under applied magnetic-field and pressure-field operation.
The unmodified alloy has poor load-bearing integrity and tends to crack under mechanical loading.
The proposed intervention is the addition of approximately 2 atomic % Nb during melting and casting.
The proposed processing includes an inert atmosphere, homogenization at approximately 950 degrees Celsius for 1–2 hours, and controlled cooling.
Nb addition followed by the proposed homogenization and cooling will form discrete, fine, coherent Nb-rich precipitates.
The Nb-rich precipitates will occur predominantly at grain boundaries and subgrain regions.
Nb will segregate to grain boundaries during casting and homogenization.
The resulting Nb-rich precipitates will be ductile.
The Nb-rich precipitates will blunt crack tips.
The Nb-rich precipitates will impede or arrest crack propagation.
Crack-tip blunting and crack arrest will increase fracture toughness relative to the unmodified alloy.
The Nb-modified alloy will have greater load-bearing capacity than the unmodified alloy.
Localization of the precipitates at boundaries will leave the bulk matrix's magnetostructural transition largely unperturbed.
Preserving the bulk magnetostructural transition will preserve the alloy's caloric performance.
The modified alloy's entropy change and transition sharpness will remain approximately 90–100% of those of the unmodified alloy.
The predicted improvements are intended to apply near room temperature, at magnetic fields up to approximately 2 T and pressures up to approximately 1 GPa.
The predicted improvements are intended to persist under mechanical loading similar to or modestly greater than baseline loading.
Excessive precipitation or intrusion of Nb-rich precipitates into the bulk matrix could compromise caloric performance.

Failure to achieve a statistically significant fracture-toughness improvement of approximately 20%, or a caloric-performance loss greater than approximately 10%, is defined as falsifying the hypothesis.
